interviewQuestions.question: Explain the exploration-exploitation trade-off with a real example.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start with the restaurant analogy: exploitation is going back to your favorite restaurant, guaranteed to be good. Exploration is trying a new place — it might be even better, or it might be a letdown, but you'll never find your new favorite if you never try anywhere new.

Concretely in a system I'd actually build: an ad-serving agent that only ever shows the ad with the historically-best click rate (pure exploitation) will never discover that a brand-new ad variant actually converts better, because it's never been shown enough to gather reliable data on it. A pure-exploration agent shows ads randomly forever and never capitalizes on what it's already learned, wasting most of its traffic on clearly-worse options.

The standard fix — epsilon-greedy — mostly shows the current best ad, but reserves a small, often-shrinking fraction of traffic to try alternatives, so the system keeps improving its estimates without giving up too much short-term reward. I'd close by noting this is the same dilemma behind multi-armed bandits and A/B testing more broadly, just formalized inside a sequential decision process.

**Testing:** whether you can ground an abstract trade-off in a concrete, business-relevant scenario rather than reciting the textbook definition.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Exploration vs exploitation

interviewQuestions.question: Why does discounting future rewards matter — couldn't you just sum up all future rewards undiscounted?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
For continuing tasks — ones with no natural endpoint, like a thermostat controller or a trading agent that runs indefinitely — summing undiscounted rewards forever is a genuine mathematical problem, not just a stylistic preference: an infinite sum of rewards can diverge to infinity for essentially any policy that earns positive reward at all, which means "the return of this policy" becomes an undefined or infinite quantity for every policy you'd want to compare. If every reasonable policy's return is infinite, you have no way to say one policy is actually better than another — the comparison the whole framework exists to make becomes meaningless. Discounting by a factor `γ < 1` guarantees the infinite sum converges to a finite value (as long as rewards are bounded), which is what makes "which policy has higher expected return" a well-defined, answerable question again.

Even for episodic tasks that do naturally terminate, where the undefined-infinite-sum problem doesn't strictly apply, discounting still earns its place for a second, more practical reason: it encodes a real preference for reward sooner rather than later, which matches how most real objectives actually work — a reward received now is generally worth more than the same reward promised for far in the future, both because of genuine time-preference and because a distant, deferred reward is subject to more uncertainty about whether it will actually materialize as planned. A low `γ` makes the agent shortsighted, over-valuing immediate reward; a `γ` close to 1 makes it value long-term consequences almost as much as immediate ones — this is a real design knob tuned to how much the task genuinely cares about long-horizon consequences.

So discounting is doing two different jobs depending on the task type: mathematical necessity for continuing tasks, and a genuine preference-encoding tool for both task types.

**Testing:** whether you understand discounting as solving a real convergence problem (not just "less weight on the future"), and can distinguish its necessity for continuing tasks from its optional-but-useful role in episodic ones.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why discounting is mathematically necessary, not just stylistic

interviewQuestions.question: You're formulating a customer-support routing problem as an MDP, using 'the current ticket's text' as the entire state. A colleague argues this violates the Markov property. Are they right, and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
They're very likely right, and it matters because violating the Markov property doesn't just make the model slightly less accurate — it breaks the theoretical foundation every standard RL algorithm relies on, since those algorithms are proven to work specifically under the assumption that the state is a sufficient statistic for the future: everything relevant to what happens next is captured in the current state, with no dependence on unmodeled history. "The current ticket's text alone" almost certainly fails this for a routing problem, because good routing decisions plausibly depend on information the text alone doesn't carry — this customer's prior ticket history, which agents are currently available and how loaded their queues are, whether this customer has escalated before, time-of-day ticket volume patterns. If any of that genuinely affects the best routing decision or the eventual reward, two tickets with identical text can have different true optimal actions depending on context the state doesn't capture — exactly what the Markov property rules out.

The practical consequence of pushing forward with an insufficient state anyway: the agent will appear to behave inconsistently or suboptimally in ways that look like a training bug, when the actual problem is that the state representation is missing information the optimal policy genuinely needs. No amount of additional training data or a better algorithm fixes a state that's fundamentally missing relevant information — the fix has to be at the state-design level, not the training level.

My recommendation: engineer the state to include what actually matters — recent interaction history for this customer, current queue/agent availability, a rolling window of similar tickets' outcomes — until the state reasonably approximates a sufficient statistic. Perfect Markov compliance is rarely achievable in real problems, but the goal is including enough context that the remaining violation is too small to meaningfully hurt the converged policy.

**Testing:** whether you understand the Markov property as a substantive modeling requirement with real consequences, not a technicality to wave away.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing a Markov-property violation in state design
